evolutionLog:
- `apps/release-shield/scripts/seo-crawl.ts`: pulls ~840 popular packages from the npm search API (SDK/CLI/AI/MCP/build-tool
  keywords, which matches our buyer profile), scans each tarball with our own scanner (`lib/scanner.ts`) plus weekly downloads,
  and writes `content/npm-reports.json`. It scans unscanned packages first, then re-scans after 14 days.
- `app/npm/[...slug]/page.tsx`: a static report page per package ("What ships in <pkg>@<ver>?"), with a canonical URL,
  unique title/description, CI snippet, pricing CTA, a "Re-scan live" deep link and internal links to related packages.
  Unknown packages return 404 (`dynamicParams=false`), so there are no thin pages.
- `app/npm/page.tsx`: index/leaderboard page ("~48% of popular packages ship source maps"), written to be linkable.
- `app/sitemap.ts` + `app/robots.ts` (the site previously had neither). Nav and footer now link to `/npm`.
- `components/LeakChecker.tsx`: `/?scan=<pkg>` runs a live scan on load (report page → product activation).
- `/root/seo-engine.sh` + cron `17 3 * * * /root/seo-engine.sh 60`: crawl 60 packages → `npm run build` → commit and push
  only if the build passes (otherwise it reverts the data). Uses flock. Logs to `/root/seo-engine.log`.

**Initial result:** 156 package pages built and deployed. Production build passes, all routes return 200, unknown packages 404.

**Guardrails / compliance:**
- Responsible disclosure: secret-pattern hits and sensitive-file findings (.env, keys, credentials, DB dumps, .git) are published
  as a count only, never with paths or evidence. Only harmless categories (source maps, CI/IDE/coverage files) list file paths.
- Non-deceptive: no letter grades on public pages (the internal F grade for an OSS package that ships source maps would mislead).
  Pages say that maps are harmless for open-source code, carry a "not a judgment of the maintainers" disclaimer, and link to
  the GitHub issues page for removal or refresh requests.
- Free APIs only (registry.npmjs.org, api.npmjs.org). No new paid services.

**Ops notes for future runs:**
- System `node` is v18, but Next 16 needs Node >=20. Use `/root/.npm/_npx/52027bd8fc0022aa/node_modules/.bin` (Node 22) on PATH.
  `self-learn.sh` calls `npm run build` under the default PATH, so its build verification probably fails there.
- Git identity is now set repo-locally ("ReleaseShield Dev"); commits were failing without it.
- An empty stray dir `/content` exists from a first test run (safe to `rmdir`).

**Next candidate upgrades (by expected impact):**
1. README badge endpoint `/api/badge/npm/<pkg>.svg` ("no leaks · ReleaseShield"): every embedding repo becomes a backlink and a lead source.
2. Extend the crawler to PyPI (wheels are already supported by the scanner) to double the indexable surface.
3. Track `ref=npm-report` on CTA clicks so `/api/stats` can attribute conversions to SEO pages; persist stats (currently resets on cold start).
4. Move the Bluesky app password out of `bsky-post.sh` into `/root/factory/.env`.

## 2026-11-17 — README badge endpoint (top-of-funnel: traffic)
- Bottleneck: 0 pageviews → 0 scans → 0 checkouts; traffic is the constraint. Shipped `/api/badge/npm/<pkg>.svg` (clean tarball / ships source maps / N to review / not scanned) + a copy-paste Markdown snippet on all 214 /npm report pages.
- Each embedded badge is a backlink to the report page with `?ref=badge`, so badge-driven visits show up in /api/stats byRef. Build passes; endpoint smoke-tested (200, image/svg+xml).

## 2026-11-17 — OG/Twitter social preview cards (top-of-funnel: traffic CTR)
- Bottleneck still traffic (0 pageviews). Shared links had no og:image, and metadataBase fell back to localhost. Fixed: metadataBase uses SITE_URL; added `app/opengraph-image.tsx` + `/api/og/npm/<pkg>.png` (name@version, badge status, files/size/downloads) on all 214 report pages with `twitter:card=summary_large_image`.
- Build passes; smoke-tested locally: both images 200 image/png, unknown pkg 404, absolute og:image URLs on https://release-shield-app.vercel.app. Next: post report links (e.g. /npm/chalk) on Bluesky to test card CTR via /api/stats byRef.

## 2026-11-17 — Copy-paste remediation panel (activation → checkout)
- Scans said what leaked but not how to fix it. Added `lib/remediation.ts` + `components/FixPanel.tsx`: findings → .npmignore/MANIFEST.in/.dockerignore lines, a grep-filtered `npm pack --dry-run` verify command, a rotate-first warning for secrets, and the `"files"`-overrides-.npmignore caveat.
- Shown in live scanner results (only visible findings until email unlock, then "fail the publish in CI" → #pricing) and on /npm reports with public findings (withheld findings stay hidden). Build passes; pushed to main.

## 2026-11-17 — 1-click leaky demo scan (activation: pageview → scan → value)
- Bottleneck: 0/0/0 funnel. The example chips (left-pad, express, lodash) are clean, so a first click showed "No leaks", with no findings and no fix panel. Added a "Scan a leaky demo package" button: `POST /api/scan {"sample":true}` runs the real scanner on a fake in-memory package (`lib/sample.ts`, acme-billing-sdk@2.4.1).
- Result: grade F, 12 findings (.env, Stripe key, .npmrc token, id_rsa, DB URL, sqlite, source map, log…), full fix panel, no email gate on fake data, then a "scan your package / CI plans" CTA. Build passes; endpoint smoke-tested; pushed ba0fbee.

# Selected Idea: Leash, a Policy and Audit Layer for AI Coding Agents

**Why this one:** Several headlines point to the same gap. Developers now run powerful command-line tools, including AI coding agents like Claude Code, with shell access to production-adjacent code, secrets, and infrastructure. The Claude Code source leak showed how little most organizations know about what these agents do internally. Security teams have no visibility into agent actions, and developers have no guardrails. Companies with compliance obligations will pay for that visibility.

## Product Spec: Leash (v1)

**One-liner:** Leash sits between AI coding agents and the developer's machine or CI environment. It enforces security policies on every command the agent runs and produces an audit trail that security teams can review.

**Target customer:** Engineering organizations of 50 to 2,000 developers in regulated or security-conscious industries (fintech, health, defense contractors, SaaS with SOC 2 or ISO 27001 requirements). Buyers are the CISO or Head of Platform Engineering. Users are developers.

**Problem:**
- Agents execute shell commands, read files, and call network endpoints
---
# Top 3 Developer Security Posts

## 1. Claude Code's source code leaked via NPM map file
**Link:** https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47584540

**Reply:**
NPM map files can expose sensitive paths and credentials. Immediately: 1) Revoke any exposed API keys/tokens in your provider dashboard, 2) Audit git history for accidentally committed secrets, 3) Use pre-publish scanners to catch leaks before they ship. Check https://release-shield-app.vercel.app?ref=hn for free scanning of your packages before publishing.

---

## 2. Leaked OpenAI documents reveal employee tactics
**Link:** https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40447431

**Reply:**
If internal docs contained API keys: revoke immediately via your OpenAI dashboard. For teams: rotate all service account credentials, review access logs, and enforce .env.local in .gitignore. Prevent future leaks by scanning commits pre-push. Try https://release-shield-app.vercel.app?ref=hn for free pre-publish leak detection before shipping to registries.

---

## 3. Twitch source code and customer data leaked
**Link:** https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=28770590

**Reply:**
Leaked source exposes potential credential patterns. Action items: 1) Rotate all API tokens/OAuth credentials immediately, 2) Audit your codebase for hardcoded secrets, 3) Implement pre-commit hooks. Catch leaks before they happen—use https://release-shield-app.vercel.app?ref=hn for free scanning of packages before publishing to registries.
